questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'write() Returns the Character Count' refers to.
questions.a: The write() method copies one string into a text file and reports how many characters it stored, counting the newline escape as a single character; numeric values must first be turned into strings before they can be written.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'write() Returns the Character Count'.
questions.a: Writing str(58) reports 2, one character per digit, because only strings may enter a text file.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'write() Returns the Character Count', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: returned = letters + 1

questions.a: 307.2 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Binary File Size from Record Count' refers to.
questions.a: A binary file grows by a fixed number of bytes per pickled record; Program 2-8 reports the size through tell(), and dividing by the record count gives the per-record size that projects the size for any number of records.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Binary File Size from Record Count'.
questions.a: Two dumped employee records produced 216 bytes, so each record occupies 108 bytes.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Binary File Size from Record Count', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: projected = total_bytes / records * new_records

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Moving the File Offset with seek' refers to.
questions.a: The tell() method reports the byte position of the file object from the start, while seek(offset, reference) jumps the object by offset bytes counted from 0 for the beginning, 1 for the current position, or 2 for the end of the file.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Moving the File Offset with seek'.
questions.a: Every read advances the offset, so Program 2-2 must rewind with seek(0) before reading again from the start.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Moving the File Offset with seek', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: new_pos = current_pos + shift

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Employee Salary Total in a Binary Record' refers to.
questions.a: Each pickled employee record stores a list of employee number, name, basic salary and allowances, with the total salary computed as basic plus allowances before the list is dumped to the binary file.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Employee Salary Total in a Binary Record'.
questions.a: The record for employee 11 holds [11, 'D N Ravi', 32600, 4400, 37000], where 37000 is basic plus allowances.

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Text File versus Binary File' refers to.
questions.a: A text file stores bytes that encode readable characters, one file line ending at an EOL such as the newline, while a binary file stores raw bytes of real content like images or executables that only specific programs can interpret.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Text File versus Binary File'.
questions.a: Opening a binary file in a text editor shows garbage because its bytes are not character codes.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Text File versus Binary File', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: text -> ASCII per character; binary -> raw byte stream

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'File Access Modes of open()' refers to.
questions.a: open(file_name, access_mode) returns a file handle whose mode controls everything: r reads from the start, w overwrites or creates, a appends at the end, a plus sign permits both reading and writing, and b switches to byte-level binary handling.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'File Access Modes of open()'.
questions.a: In r, r+ and w modes the object starts at the beginning; in a and a+ it starts at the end.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'File Access Modes of open()', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: r/w/a plus optional + and b, with the offset at start or end

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Reading Methods: read, readline, readlines' refers to.
questions.a: Three methods drain a text file: read(n) takes n bytes or the whole file, readline() returns one line up to its newline, and readlines() returns every line as the elements of a list of strings.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Reading Methods: read, readline, readlines'.
questions.a: Looping over the file object or calling readline() repeatedly ends when an empty string signals end of file.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Reading Methods: read, readline, readlines', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: readlines() -> list of lines; readline() -> one line; read() -> whole text

concepts.title: Pickling and the dump, load Methods

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Pickling and the dump, load Methods' refers to.
questions.a: The pickle module serialises a Python object into a byte stream for a binary file: dump(object, file_object) writes it while the file is open in wb mode, and load(file_object) rebuilds the object from a file opened in rb mode.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Pickling and the dump, load Methods'.
questions.a: Pickling stores the object's structure as well as its data, so a dumped list loads back as a list.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Pickling and the dump, load Methods', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: dump -> object to bytes; load -> bytes back to object
